note:
The patient is a 75-year-old male seen in the orthopedic clinic for follow-up of right knee osteoarthritis. He returned about ten days ago from a three-week trip abroad that included two long-haul flights of more than ten hours each, and over the past week his right knee pain has been worse than usual. He describes stiffness after sitting through the flights and a sharp ache on stairs, rated 6 out of 10 at its worst. He denies fever, redness, warmth, and any fall or twisting injury. Because of the prolonged sitting during travel, I specifically asked about clot symptoms, and he denies calf pain, chest pain, and shortness of breath. He has had no new swelling in either leg.

His history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and acetaminophen 650 mg three times daily as needed. While traveling he also took over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a day for the knee.

Vitals today are BP 132/78, HR 76, temperature 98.4 F, and SpO2 97% on room air. On exam he walks with a mildly antalgic gait. The right knee has a small effusion, medial joint line tenderness, and crepitus with flexion, with range of motion from 0 to 120 degrees and no warmth or erythema. The ligaments are stable. Both calves are soft and nontender with symmetric circumference. The left knee shows only mild crepitus.

Standing weight-bearing X-rays of both knees today show medial joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis on the right, consistent with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 3, with milder changes on the left. Serum creatinine today is 1.3 mg/dL with an eGFR of 55.

Impression is a flare of right knee osteoarthritis after prolonged immobility and increased walking while traveling, with no clinical evidence of septic arthritis or deep vein thrombosis. Given his age, diabetes, lisinopril use, and borderline kidney function, I advised him to stop ibuprofen and avoid all NSAIDs. I increased acetaminophen to 1000 mg three times daily on a scheduled basis, not to exceed 3 grams a day. After discussing risks and benefits, I performed an intra-articular corticosteroid injection of the right knee today using triamcinolone 40 mg with lidocaine, and he tolerated it well. He was told that his blood sugars may run higher for several days and that he should check his glucose more often. I referred him to physical therapy for quadriceps strengthening. He will return in six weeks, sooner for calf swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath.
summary: A 75-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was seen for worsening right knee pain after a three-week trip abroad with long flights. He denies fever, calf pain, chest pain and shortness of breath, and examination showed a small right knee effusion, medial joint line tenderness and crepitus without warmth or erythema. X-rays showed grade 3 osteoarthritis on the right, and creatinine was 1.3 mg/dL with an eGFR of 55. The impression was a flare of right knee osteoarthritis without evidence of septic arthritis or deep vein thrombosis. Ibuprofen was stopped, acetaminophen was increased to 1000 mg three times daily, a triamcinolone injection was given, and physical therapy and six-week follow-up were arranged.

note:
Nurse: Next up is a 6-year-old male here with his mother for ear pain.
Doctor: Hi buddy. Tell me what's going on with your ear.
Patient: My right ear hurts. It hurts a lot.
Family member: It started yesterday. He had a runny nose and a cough all last week, and then last night he woke up crying and holding his ear.
Doctor: Did he have a fever?
Family member: He felt warm last night, so I gave him children's ibuprofen and it helped a little.
Doctor: Any drainage from the ear, vomiting, or diarrhea?
Family member: No drainage. No vomiting and no diarrhea. He is eating and drinking okay.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines? And does he take anything every day?
Family member: No allergies to medicines, and he takes nothing every day. He is healthy otherwise.
Doctor: Okay. His temperature is 100.2 and his weight is 22 kilograms. Let me look in your ears, buddy. On otoscopy the left eardrum looks normal. The right eardrum is red and bulging, and it doesn't move when I puff a little air on it. There is no swelling or tenderness behind the ear. His throat is mildly red, his lungs are clear, and his heart sounds normal.
Doctor: This is acute otitis media of the right ear, probably following that cold. I'm going to start amoxicillin 1000 mg twice a day for seven days. Keep giving the ibuprofen, 200 mg every six hours as needed for pain or fever, with food.
Family member: Okay. When should he start feeling better?
Doctor: Within two to three days. If he is not better by then, or if you see ear drainage, swelling behind the ear, or a high fever, call us or bring him back. Otherwise he does not need a follow-up visit.
Family member: Thank you.
summary: A 6-year-old male was brought in by his mother with right ear pain that began yesterday after a week of runny nose and cough, and he felt warm last night. He has had no ear drainage, vomiting or diarrhea, and he has no medicine allergies. His temperature was 100.2 and the right eardrum was red and bulging and did not move with an air puff, while the left eardrum was normal, the throat mildly red and the lungs clear. The diagnosis is acute otitis media of the right ear. Amoxicillin 1000 mg twice a day for seven days was started, ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed was advised for pain or fever, and return precautions were given.

soap.subjective: 6-year-old male with right ear pain since yesterday, preceded by a runny nose and cough for a week. He woke up crying and holding his ear last night and felt warm, and children's ibuprofen helped a little. No ear drainage, vomiting, or diarrhea; eating and drinking okay. No allergies to medicines, takes nothing daily, and is otherwise healthy.
soap.objective: Temperature 100.2, weight 22 kilograms. On otoscopy the left eardrum is normal; the right eardrum is red and bulging and does not move with a puff of air. No swelling or tenderness behind the ear. Throat mildly red, lungs clear, heart sounds normal.
soap.assessment: Acute otitis media of the right ear, probably following a recent cold.
plan: Start amoxicillin 1000 mg twice a day for seven days
Ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed for pain or fever, given with food
Expect improvement within two to three days
Call or return if not better, or for ear drainage, swelling behind the ear, or a high fever
No routine follow-up visit needed

note:
56-year-old female, derm clinic, c/o changing mole L upper back
CC: changing pigmented lesion L upper back, noticed by husband x ~3 mo, getting bigger/darker
HPI: pt cannot see her back herself. Husband says it was flat and tan before, now raised in center, darker, bigger. Denies itch, bleeding, pain, ulceration. No prior skin bx. No hx melanoma. FH: mother w/ melanoma.
ROS: no fever, wt loss, night sweats, headache, or bone pain
Sun hx: several blistering sunburns as teen, no tanning bed use, 20 yrs outdoor gardening
Social: nonsmoker, rare EtOH
PMH: HTN, T2DM, actinic keratoses
Meds: amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BID. NKDA.
Vitals: BP 128/76, HR 72
Labs per PCP 2 wk ago: A1c 6.4%, Cr 0.8
Exam: full skin exam done
- L upper back: 9 mm asymmetric macule w/ irregular borders, variegated brown/black/blue-gray, central papule
- dermoscopy: atypical network, blue-white veil, irregular streaks
- other nevi: benign, symmetric, no other atypical lesions
- face: multiple rough scaly erythematous papules on forehead and cheeks c/w AKs
- no cervical, axillary or inguinal LAD
Dx: changing pigmented lesion L upper back, r/o melanoma. AKs face.
Discussed dx, bx procedure, risks (bleeding, infection, scar) and benefits. Pt verbalized understanding, consent signed.
Tx:
- excisional bx w/ 2 mm margins today, lidocaine 1% w/ epi, closed w/ 4-0 nylon x 5 sutures, pt tolerated well, no complications
- path pending, call pt in 1 wk w/ result. If melanoma, refer to surg onc for WLE +/- SLNB
- wound care: keep dry 24 h, then petrolatum and bandage daily, no heavy lifting x 2 wk

summary: A 56-year-old female with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and actinic keratoses was seen for a pigmented lesion on the left upper back that her husband noticed getting bigger and darker over about three months. She denies itch, bleeding, pain and ulceration, and her mother had melanoma. Examination showed a 9 mm asymmetric variegated macule with a central papule and atypical dermoscopy, with no lymphadenopathy and rough scaly papules on the face. The impression is a changing pigmented lesion, rule out melanoma, plus facial actinic keratoses. An excisional biopsy was done with pathology pending, fluorouracil 5% cream was started, and follow-up is in 2 weeks.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 32-year-old male referred for urinary urgency and frequency. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah, for about eight months now I feel like I have to pee all the time. During the day it's probably ten or twelve times, and I wake up two or three times at night. Sometimes the urge comes on so fast that I leak a little before I get to the bathroom. That happens maybe twice a week.
Doctor: So that's urgency with some urge incontinence, and the night-time waking is called nocturia. Any burning when you urinate, blood in the urine, fever, or back pain?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: How about a weak stream, or feeling like you can't empty your bladder?
Patient: No, the stream is fine.
Doctor: How much caffeine do you drink?
Patient: Probably four coffees a day, plus an energy drink in the afternoon.
Doctor: Okay, that matters. Any medical conditions, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have anxiety. I take sertraline 50 mg once a day. That's it.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: Yes, oxybutynin. A couple of years ago an urgent care doctor gave it to me for the same problem, and I broke out in hives on my chest and arms. I stopped it right away.
Doctor: Thank you, I'm documenting oxybutynin as a drug allergy, so we'll avoid it. Now your results. Blood pressure today is 124/78 and pulse is 72. Your belly is soft and not tender, with no tenderness over the bladder or in the flanks. Your urinalysis today is clean, with no blood, no infection, and no sugar. The bladder scan after you urinated showed only 30 milliliters left behind, so you are emptying well.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is overactive bladder. There's no sign of infection or anything blocking the flow. First, cut your coffee down to one or two cups a day and stop the energy drinks, and try timed voiding every two to three hours while keeping a three-day bladder diary. I'm also going to start mirabegron 25 mg once daily. It works in a different way from oxybutynin, so it should avoid the problem you had with hives. It can raise blood pressure a little, so we'll recheck your pressure at the next visit.
Patient: Okay. When do I come back?
Doctor: In six weeks. Call sooner if you have fever, burning, blood in the urine, or you can't pass urine.
Patient: Sounds good.
summary: A 32-year-old male was seen for eight months of urinary urgency, ten to twelve daytime voids, nocturia two or three times a night and occasional urge leakage, with no burning, blood in the urine, fever or back pain. He drinks about four coffees and an energy drink daily and takes sertraline 50 mg once a day for anxiety. He has a documented allergy to oxybutynin that caused hives. Blood pressure was 124/78, the abdomen was benign, urinalysis was clean and the bladder scan showed 30 milliliters left behind. The diagnosis is overactive bladder, and he will cut caffeine, start timed voiding with a bladder diary, begin mirabegron 25 mg once daily, and return in six weeks.

soap.subjective: 32-year-old male referred for urinary urgency and frequency for about eight months, voiding ten or twelve times a day and waking two or three times at night. Sometimes leaks a little before reaching the bathroom, about twice a week. Denies burning, blood in the urine, fever, back pain, and a weak stream. Drinks about four coffees a day plus an energy drink. Has anxiety and takes sertraline 50 mg once a day. Allergic to oxybutynin, which caused hives on the chest and arms a couple of years ago.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 124/78, pulse 72. Abdomen soft and not tender, with no tenderness over the bladder or in the flanks. Urinalysis clean with no blood, no infection, and no sugar. Bladder scan after voiding showed 30 milliliters left behind.
soap.assessment: Overactive bladder with urgency, urge incontinence and nocturia, with no sign of infection or obstruction. Anxiety. Oxybutynin allergy documented.
plan: Cut coffee down to one or two cups a day and stop energy drinks
Timed voiding every two to three hours and a three-day bladder diary
Start mirabegron 25 mg once daily, a different mechanism from oxybutynin, and avoid oxybutynin
Recheck blood pressure at the next visit because mirabegron can raise it
Follow up in six weeks
Call sooner for fever, burning, blood in the urine, or inability to pass urine

note:
Infectious Diseases Consultation, Emergency Department

Reason for consult: Herpes zoster in an 81-year-old female with chronic kidney disease, for antiviral dosing and pain management.
Requesting service: Emergency Medicine.

HPI: The patient is an 81-year-old female who presented to the ED with three days of burning pain along her left lower chest wall, followed over the last 24 hours by a blistering, painful rash that wraps from her mid back toward the front of the left side. She rates the pain 8 out of 10, describes it as burning and stabbing with light touch hypersensitivity, and says it kept her awake all night. She denies fever, chills, headache, vision changes, eye pain, facial droop, weakness of the legs, and difficulty urinating. She has had no known contact with anyone with chickenpox and does not recall ever having shingles before.

Yesterday she was seen at urgent care and was started on valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for seven days. She has taken three doses so far. She was also told to take ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain, which she has been taking since the rash began.

Social history: She still works part-time rotating shifts at a hospital laundry, alternating day and night weeks, and her sleep and meal times change from week to week. She admits she is unsure when to take pills on night-shift days and has missed some doses of her home medications. Her daughter is at the bedside.

Past medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypothyroidism, and hyperlipidemia.

Home medications: On initial review the patient reported taking metformin 1000 mg twice daily, but when her daughter brought in the pill bottles, the correct dose was confirmed as 500 mg twice daily. Her other medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, which her primary care physician reduced from 20 mg last month because of a rising creatinine, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. No known drug allergies.

Exam: Temperature 98.6 F, HR 88, BP 146/84, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air. She is uncomfortable but alert and oriented. Skin shows grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a band-like distribution over the left T7 dermatome from the mid back to near the sternum, some becoming pustular, none crossing the midline. There are no hemorrhagic or necrotic lesions and no signs of bacterial superinfection. The face, scalp, and nose are clear and the eyes are normal. No lymphadenopathy. Motor strength and sensation are intact except for allodynia in the affected dermatome.

Data: WBC 8.9, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 245, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.3), eGFR 36, potassium 4.4, glucose 168. A swab of vesicle fluid was sent for varicella zoster virus PCR. No imaging was obtained.

Impression: Acute herpes zoster of the left T7 dermatome, uncomplicated, without ophthalmic or neurologic involvement, presenting within 72 hours of rash onset in an immunocompetent host with CKD stage 3b. The valacyclovir dose she was given is too high for an eGFR of 36, and ibuprofen should not be used given her CKD, ACE inhibitor, and diabetes. Her risk of postherpetic neuralgia is elevated by her age and severe pain.

Recommendations:
1. Reduce valacyclovir to 1000 mg twice daily to finish a total of seven days. Take doses about 12 hours apart, starting from whenever she wakes up, and set phone alarms so the schedule follows her shifts.
2. Discontinue ibuprofen and avoid all NSAIDs.
3. Start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime, taken before her main sleep period whether that is day or night, with slow titration only if needed and renal dosing. Counsel on drowsiness and fall risk.
4. Use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for additional pain relief, not exceeding 3 grams a day.
5. Continue her other home medications at the doses above and repeat a BMP in one week.
6. Keep the lesions covered. She should avoid contact with pregnant women, infants, and immunocompromised people and stay off work until all lesions are crusted.
7. She should receive the recombinant zoster vaccine after the rash has resolved.
8. Okay for discharge from the ED. ID clinic follow-up in one week. Return for any rash near the eye, fever, confusion, spreading redness, or uncontrolled pain.
summary: An 81-year-old female with chronic kidney disease stage 3b, diabetes, hypertension and hypothyroidism presented to the ED with three days of burning left chest wall pain and a one-day blistering band-like rash, and she works rotating shifts. Examination showed grouped vesicles over the left T7 dermatome with allodynia and no eye, facial or neurologic involvement, and eGFR was 36. The impression is uncomplicated acute herpes zoster. Valacyclovir was reduced from 1000 mg three times daily to 1000 mg twice daily, ibuprofen was stopped, and gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime and acetaminophen were added. She should cover the lesions, stay off work until crusted, and follow up in the ID clinic in one week.

note:
Nurse: Rooming a 13-year-old male with his mother, wheezing and trouble breathing. Triage vitals: temperature 98.9, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Peak flow is 210, which is about 55 percent of his predicted value.
Doctor: Thanks. Hi there, I hear you've been having a hard time breathing. Tell me what's going on.
Patient: I keep coughing and wheezing, especially at night, and my chest feels tight. I can't run at all, and even the stairs at school make me out of breath.
Family member: It started about three days ago after a cold. He's been using his rescue inhaler every three or four hours, and last night he used it like six times.
Doctor: Does the rescue inhaler help?
Patient: A little, for maybe an hour.
Doctor: Any fever, vomiting, chest pain, or swelling of the lips?
Family member: No fever, no vomiting, and he says no chest pain or swelling of the lips.
Doctor: What does he take every day for his asthma?
Family member: He's supposed to take Flovent, the 44 microgram one, two puffs twice a day. Actually, wait, let me look at the box. It says 110 micrograms, two puffs twice a day. Sorry, that's the right one.
Doctor: And is he actually taking it?
Family member: Honestly, no. It ran out about two months ago. The refill was almost 90 dollars with our new insurance plan and we just couldn't afford it right now. We've only been using the albuterol because it's cheaper.
Doctor: I really appreciate you telling me that. It's very common, and it's probably a big reason he's flaring up. Is he still on the montelukast?
Family member: No, he stopped that last spring because it gave him bad dreams.
Doctor: Okay. Anything else?
Family member: Cetirizine 10 mg once a day for his runny nose in the spring, and a cream for the eczema on his elbows when it flares.
Doctor: Okay, so the cetirizine is for his allergic rhinitis, and he has eczema too. Any allergies to medications?
Family member: No drug allergies.
Doctor: Alright. Let me listen to your chest. He is working a bit hard to breathe, using his neck muscles a little. I hear diffuse expiratory wheezes with decreased air movement at both bases, no stridor. His throat is clear, and I see dry patches on both elbows. Heart is fast but regular. We also got a chest X-ray, and it shows some hyperinflation but no pneumonia.
Doctor: This is an asthma exacerbation, moderate, triggered by a cold and made worse because he has been without his controller medicine for two months. We'll give him an albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer treatment, three back to back over the next hour, plus a dose of oral prednisone.
Nurse: He finished the third nebulizer. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air and peak flow is 330, about 85 percent of predicted.
Doctor: Good, he sounds much better and the wheezing is mild now. Here is the plan for home. Prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days. Albuterol, two puffs with the spacer every four hours for the next two days, instead of just as needed, then back to as needed. Restart fluticasone 110 micrograms, two puffs twice a day with the spacer, and rinse his mouth afterward. I'll send the generic and our social worker will help with a patient assistance program and a 90-day supply so the cost doesn't get in the way again. Let's officially stop the montelukast, and continue the cetirizine 10 mg daily and the eczema cream as before. I'm also giving you a written asthma action plan.
Family member: That helps a lot, thank you.
Doctor: See his pediatrician in two to three days. Go to the ER if he can't speak a full sentence, his lips look blue, or he needs albuterol more often than every four hours.
Family member: Understood.
summary: A 13-year-old male with asthma, allergic rhinitis and eczema came to urgent care with three days of wheezing, cough and chest tightness after a cold, and he had been without his controller inhaler for two months because of cost. His heart rate was 112, respiratory rate 26 and oxygen saturation 93%, with diffuse expiratory wheezes, and a chest X-ray showed hyperinflation without pneumonia. After three nebulizer treatments his oxygen saturation was 97% and peak flow rose from 55 to 85 percent of predicted. The diagnosis is a moderate asthma exacerbation. He went home on prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days, scheduled albuterol and restarted fluticasone 110 micrograms, with montelukast stopped and social work help with cost.

soap.subjective: 13-year-old male with asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eczema brought in by his mother with three days of coughing, wheezing, and chest tightness after a cold, worse at night, with shortness of breath on stairs. Using his rescue inhaler every three or four hours and about six times last night, with only brief relief. Denies fever, vomiting, chest pain, and swelling of the lips. Controller inhaler fluticasone 110 micrograms, two puffs twice a day, ran out about two months ago and was not refilled because of cost, so he has used only albuterol. Montelukast was stopped last spring because of bad dreams. Takes cetirizine 10 mg once a day and uses a cream for eczema. No drug allergies.
soap.objective: Triage: temperature 98.9, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, peak flow 210 (about 55 percent of predicted). Working a bit hard to breathe with mild neck muscle use, diffuse expiratory wheezes, decreased air movement at both bases, no stridor. Throat clear, dry patches on both elbows, heart fast but regular. Chest X-ray shows some hyperinflation but no pneumonia. After three albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer treatments, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, peak flow 330 (about 85 percent of predicted), mild wheezing.
soap.assessment: Moderate asthma exacerbation triggered by a cold and worsened by two months without controller medicine because of cost. Allergic rhinitis and eczema.
plan: Albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer treatments, three back to back over the hour, plus a dose of oral prednisone in clinic
Prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days
Albuterol two puffs with the spacer every four hours for the next two days, then back to as needed
Restart fluticasone 110 micrograms, two puffs twice a day with the spacer, and rinse his mouth afterward
Prescribe the generic; social worker to help with a patient assistance program and a 90-day supply
Stop montelukast; continue cetirizine 10 mg daily and the eczema cream
Written asthma action plan
See his pediatrician in two to three days

note:
Rheumatology inpatient progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is a 75-year-old male admitted with severe bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness who is being followed for polymyalgia rheumatica. A professional Spanish interpreter was used for the entire visit, and the history below was confirmed through the interpreter.

Overnight there were no events and he slept better than on previous nights. This morning he reports that his shoulder and hip pain is much better, about 3 out of 10 compared with 9 out of 10 on admission, and morning stiffness now lasts about 20 minutes instead of several hours. He walked to the bathroom with the physical therapist for the first time since admission.

His symptoms began about five weeks ago, shortly after he returned from a three-week trip to Mexico to visit relatives. Through the interpreter he denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision changes, cough, and diarrhea.

Medication history: At first he said he was taking naproxen 250 mg twice daily for the pain. After the interpreter clarified the label with him, the correct dose is naproxen 500 mg twice daily, taken over the counter for the last four weeks. His other home medications are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Hospital medications: Prednisone was started at 20 mg daily on admission and was decreased to 15 mg daily today because of his brisk response. Naproxen was stopped on admission. Metformin was held on admission and was resumed today. Calcium carbonate 600 mg twice daily and vitamin D3 1000 units daily were started for bone protection. Because of his recent travel and the start of steroids, he is receiving ivermectin 200 mcg/kg once daily for two days as prophylaxis for Strongyloides while the serology is pending.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.2 F, BP 138/82, HR 74, RR 16, and SpO2 97% on room air. He is comfortable. There is no temporal artery tenderness and the temporal pulses are palpable. Active shoulder abduction has improved to 120 degrees from 60 degrees on admission. There is no synovitis in the hands, wrists, or knees and no rash. Lungs are clear.

Data: ESR is 52 mm/hr today, down from 78 on admission, and CRP is 21 mg/L, down from 62. Hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Fasting glucose was 212 mg/dL this morning. ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and CK were normal or negative. QuantiFERON and hepatitis B surface antigen are negative. Strongyloides IgG is pending. Chest X-ray is clear.

Impression: Polymyalgia rheumatica with a brisk response to prednisone and no features of giant cell arteritis. Infectious and rheumatologic screens are negative so far. Steroid-associated hyperglycemia in the setting of type 2 diabetes mellitus. He also has hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Plan: Continue prednisone 15 mg daily and taper slowly at outpatient rheumatology follow-up in two weeks. Finish ivermectin and follow up the Strongyloides IgG. Continue calcium and vitamin D3 and obtain an outpatient DEXA scan. Check fingerstick glucose before meals and at bedtime and add correction insulin as needed. Avoid NSAIDs from now on. Continue lisinopril, atorvastatin, and omeprazole. Review giant cell arteritis warning signs with him through the interpreter before discharge. Anticipate discharge tomorrow.

His pain is down from 9 to 3 out of 10 on prednisone, now reduced from 20 mg to 15 mg daily, and he denies fever, headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication. ESR fell from 78 to 52, QuantiFERON and hepatitis B surface antigen are negative, and fasting glucose is 212 mg/dL. The impression is polymyalgia rheumatica with a brisk steroid response and steroid-associated hyperglycemia. Naproxen, taken at 500 mg twice daily after clarification, was stopped, and ivermectin, calcium and vitamin D3 were started with discharge anticipated tomorrow.

note: Geriatrics consult dictation on the hospital ward. This is an 85-year-old female who was admitted two days ago for observation after a fall and whom we were asked to see for urinary incontinence. She tells me the leakage began about two weeks ago, correction, about three weeks ago. She leaks urine with a strong sudden urge before she can reach the toilet about four to five times a day, and she wakes up twice a night to void. She denies burning with urination, blood in the urine, fever, and back pain. She denies leaking with coughing or sneezing, so I do not think there is a stress component. Her only chronic problem is hypertension, for which she takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily in the afternoon. She drinks about three cups of tea and two cups of coffee a day. Vitals this morning are blood pressure 134/76 and heart rate 72. On exam the abdomen is soft and nontender with no suprapubic fullness, and there is no stool impaction on rectal exam. The cognitive screen is unremarkable. Urinalysis is negative for infection and the post void residual by bladder scan is 40 mL. My impression is urge urinary incontinence, likely related to her caffeine intake, her afternoon diuretic dosing, and reduced mobility in the hospital. Plan is to have nursing offer toileting every two hours while she is awake, keep a bladder diary, limit caffeine to one cup of coffee in the morning, move the hydrochlorothiazide to the morning, and avoid bladder antispasmodic medications because of her age and the risk of confusion. I will also request physical therapy for pelvic floor exercises. She can follow up in the geriatrics clinic after discharge.

The plan is scheduled toileting, a bladder diary, less caffeine, moving hydrochlorothiazide to the morning, avoiding bladder antispasmodics, and physical therapy.

note:
The patient is a 92-year-old male seen in geriatrics clinic for advance care planning and follow-up of his chronic conditions. He lives alone in his own home and has limited social support: a neighbor checks on him a few times a week and a son who lives in another state calls on weekends. He wants to remain at home for as long as possible.

His history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, and mild cognitive impairment. Over the past two weeks he has noticed more shortness of breath when walking to his mailbox and mild ankle swelling, and his home weight is up about 4 pounds. He denies chest pain, orthopnea, and dizziness. His medications are furosemide 20 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, and diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly, which he has taken for years to help him sleep.

Vitals today are BP 118/64, HR 70 and irregular, SpO2 95% on room air, and weight 168 pounds. He has mild bibasilar crackles and 1+ pitting edema of both ankles, with no jugular venous distension. His MoCA score today is 24 out of 30. He explained his conditions and the choices in his own words and showed good decision-making capacity. Labs from two weeks ago show creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with an eGFR of 38, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and potassium 4.3.

We spent 40 minutes on advance care planning. He understands that his heart and kidney disease are likely to progress. His goals are to stay in his home, avoid long hospital stays, and keep his independence. He would accept hospital admission for treatable problems such as pneumonia or fluid overload, but he does not want CPR or a breathing machine. He named his son as his health care proxy. We completed a POLST form today that documents DNR/DNI with selective treatment, and he signed it. Copies will go to his son and be kept on his refrigerator.

Impression is mild volume overload from heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, completed advance care planning, and a sedating anticholinergic that is not appropriate with his cognitive impairment. I increased furosemide from 20 mg to 40 mg daily and will recheck a basic metabolic panel in one week. I stopped diphenhydramine and reviewed sleep hygiene. He will continue apixaban and metoprolol succinate. I am referring him to home health nursing, social work, and palliative care for added support, and social work will help arrange a medical alert pendant and home meal delivery. He will weigh himself daily and call the clinic if his weight goes up more than 3 pounds in two days. Follow-up is in two weeks.
summary: A 92-year-old male who lives alone with limited social support was seen for advance care planning and chronic disease follow-up, with heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease and mild cognitive impairment. He has had two weeks of more shortness of breath and ankle swelling with a 4 pound weight gain, bibasilar crackles and pitting edema, and he showed good decision-making capacity with a MoCA of 24 out of 30. He chose to stay at home, accept treatable hospital care, decline CPR and intubation, and completed a POLST form. Furosemide was increased to 40 mg daily, diphenhydramine was stopped, and home health, social work and palliative care referrals were made with follow-up in two weeks.

note:
This is a dictation for a gastroenterology follow-up visit on a 60-year-old female with ulcerative colitis, last seen about eight months ago, who returns with a flare. She was diagnosed with extensive ulcerative colitis about ten years ago and had been well controlled on mesalamine. Over the last three weeks she has had five to six loose stools a day with visible blood on about half of them, along with urgency and lower abdominal cramping, and she is waking once or twice a night to have a bowel movement. She denies fever, vomiting, weight loss, joint pain, eye redness, and mouth sores, and she has not had any recent antibiotics or sick contacts.

She tells me she takes mesalamine delayed release 2.4 grams once daily, correction, she is actually taking only 1.2 grams once daily, one tablet, because she has been rationing her supply. The prescribed dose is 4.8 grams once daily. Her copay went up after her insurance changed, and the pharmacy told her the cost is now about 180 dollars a month, which she cannot afford. She works rotating shifts at a warehouse, alternating day weeks and night weeks, and with this irregular schedule she often forgets doses or skips them when she comes off a night shift. She has also been using over-the-counter loperamide 2 mg up to four times a day to control the diarrhea.

Other medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteopenia. Her other medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily, and she reports taking all of them. She has no known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 88, temperature 98.6 F, and weight 142 pounds, which is stable. On exam she looks well and mucous membranes are moist. The abdomen is soft with mild left lower quadrant tenderness, no distension, and no rebound or guarding, and bowel sounds are normal.

Labs this week show hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, MCV 78, ferritin 9 ng/mL, WBC 9.6, platelets 412, CRP 14 mg/L, and albumin 3.8. Fecal calprotectin is 640 micrograms per gram. Stool C diff PCR and stool culture are both negative.

My impression is a mild to moderate flare of extensive ulcerative colitis, caused by under-dosing of mesalamine because of cost and her irregular shift schedule, along with iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss. Plan is to increase mesalamine back to 4.8 grams once daily, taken as a single dose with food when she wakes up, regardless of which shift she is working. I will prescribe the generic as a 90-day supply and refer her to social work for pharmacy assistance programs. I am also starting budesonide MMX 9 mg once daily, taken when she first wakes up, for eight weeks. She should stop the loperamide. I am starting ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily for the iron deficiency. I am ordering a colonoscopy with biopsies in eight to twelve weeks after the flare settles to reassess disease extent and screen for dysplasia, and a repeat CBC and CRP in four weeks. She should call right away for more than eight stools a day, fever, heavy bleeding, or severe abdominal pain. Follow up in four weeks.
summary: A 60-year-old female with ulcerative colitis, hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD and osteopenia returned with three weeks of five to six bloody loose stools a day. She had been rationing mesalamine, taking only 1.2 grams once daily of a prescribed 4.8 grams, because of cost, and her rotating night and day shifts cause missed doses. Fecal calprotectin was 640, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL and ferritin 9, with negative stool C diff PCR and culture. The impression is a mild to moderate flare of extensive ulcerative colitis with iron deficiency anemia. Mesalamine was increased to 4.8 grams once daily, budesonide MMX and ferrous sulfate were started, loperamide was stopped, and colonoscopy with social work referral for cost help was arranged.
